g.text: The two wire codecs — msgpack is what Terraform speaks, JSON is what it stores and shows
a CtyValue, and the CtyType to write it against
Both codecs are type-directed in both directions: the wire cannot tell
a list from a set from a tuple, so the type is supplied, never guessed.
deep mark check, once, up front
shallow mark check at every level, for the path
integer-keyed, only the keys that are set:
the dynamic envelope → [type-spec JSON as bytes, value]
back: parse_tf_type_to_ctytype, then decode against it
deep mark check, then convert() if not conformant
an unknown is an error here, not a null
numbers: infinity refused; plain decimal only
objects: attributes sorted, only those present
capsules: a Bytes buffer as base64, any other refused
dynamic: an object of value + type
primitives coerce through go-cty's small explicit table
object: an undeclared attribute is an
dynamic: an object carrying both value and type
tfplugin6.DynamicValue has a msgpack field and a json field.
There is no third field, which is why marks cannot travel here.
shallowly at every level below. The per-level check is what supplies the path to the
offending value, but it only sees what the encoder descends into — and it never descends into an unknown,
which a container becomes as soon as any element is unknown. Without the deep pre-check, a marked unknown
inside a list serialized silently, dropping exactly the flag the refusal exists to protect.
An integer inside int64 becomes a msgpack integer; outside it, the decimal text. A non-integer becomes a
only when the conversion is exact
, tested as Decimal(float(d)) == d. Testing against str(float(d))
instead answered "nothing lost" for 0.1 — whose true binary value is 0.1000000000000000055… — so this wrote a
float where go-cty writes the string "0.1". A perpetual diff on every non-integer attribute.
: go-cty's number is a big.Float, which has none, so the text "NaN" this used to
write comes back from go-cty as "number is required". ±Inf is fine and round-trips as a float64.
is irrelevant, because one byte is what makes the encoding a msgpack fixext1.
An empty payload is legal msgpack and decodes to the same value, but it is c7 00 00 — a different
serialization of the same unknown. Terraform compares serialized state, so the bytes have to match too.
string_prefix is capped at 256 bytes and then re-trimmed by safe_known_prefix, so the cut cannot land
mid-grapheme-cluster. Each number bound is written as [number, inclusive] through the ordinary number
serializer, matching go-cty byte-for-byte — raw UTF-8 digit bytes would decode to the same value but not
the same bytes, and Terraform compares serialized state. An empty payload falls back to the ext-0 form.
A dynamic slot carries no type of its own, so the concrete type has to travel beside the value or the far
side has nothing to decode against.
This holds for an unknown and a null too
branch is taken before either: checking knownness first sent unknown-of-string as a bare d4 00 00 and
null-of-string as a bare c0, and go-cty reads both of those back as
Converting is go-cty's documented behaviour for a non-conformant value. The mark check runs
conversion, because conversion rebuilds a value and a rebuilt value that quietly lost a mark would then
There is no JSON spelling for "not yet decided", and writing null would turn a value that has not been
computed into one that definitively has no value.
Go's encoding/json escapes < > & U+2028 U+2029 by default and Python's json does not. Those bytes end up in
state files that are compared textually, so a < written two ways is a diff on every plan. Non-ASCII is
in the table: Go writes it raw.
A Decimal that remembers the digits it was written with. Unmarshalling a JSON number into a string yields
, so 1.50 stays "1.50" and 1e2 stays "1e2" — neither is recoverable from the parsed number.
string accepts a string, a number's literal text, or a bool; number accepts a number or a string holding
one; bool accepts a bool or a string holding one. Every other combination is refused. Refusing the lot
instead rejects state and plan JSON that go-cty reads without complaint.
JSON gives no guarantee that an array's elements share a type, and a list would have to invent one.
elements by value and every other element type by the bytes of
makeSetHashBytes, which is a different comparison — a set of tuples writes [12] before [1]. That order
